title: Density and material volume
prior_knowledge_summary: Three coplanar forces in equilibrium can be represented by a closed head-to-tail triangle.
Geometry or components can be used to determine an unknown equilibrium force.
SI prefixes and geometric volume relationships can be used to express measurements in consistent units.
new_learning: Use density as mass per unit volume.
Rearrange the density relationship to determine mass or material volume.
Convert density and volume units consistently before calculation.
Distinguish the volume of material present from the outer volume occupied by an object with gaps or cut-outs.

blocks.heading: Same size, very different mass
content: Imagine two sealed cubes with exactly the same outer volume. One has a mass of 0.16 kg and the other has a mass of 1.25 kg. Their shapes and sizes match, yet lifting them feels completely different.
Volume alone cannot describe the material. We need a quantity that compares how much mass is packed into each unit of volume.
Predict which cube has the greater value of this quantity, and explain your prediction without using a formula yet.

figure.purpose: Create a same-volume, different-mass puzzle that motivates density.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of two equal-sized cubes on separate balance pans. Label their equal volume and masses 0.16 kg and 1.25 kg. Use one colour for equal dimensions and another for the mass readings. Do not name density or state which value is greater.
figure.alt_text: Two cubes have the same volume but masses of 0.16 kilograms and 1.25 kilograms.

blocks.heading: Compare mass for each unit of volume
content: The formal definition of density is: mass per unit volume. It asks how much mass belongs to each cubic metre, cubic centimetre, or other stated unit of volume.

The formula to remember is density equals mass divided by volume. The symbol rho is used for density. In SI units, mass is in kilograms and volume is in cubic metres, so density is in kilograms per cubic metre.
For equal volumes, the object with more mass has greater density. For equal masses, the object with less volume has greater density. Both comparisons come from the same mass-per-volume idea.

symbols: rho is the density of the material.
m is the mass of the material.
V is the volume of material present.
formula_to_remember.units: In SI units, rho is in kg m^-3, m is in kg and V is in m^3.

figure.purpose: Show density as a comparison of mass assigned to equal volume cells.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison strip containing two equal 1 cm cubed cells. Place a few simple mass tokens in one and many in the other. Add sparse labels equal volume, smaller mass and larger mass, then a separate formula card rho equals m over V. Avoid particle or molecular claims.
figure.alt_text: Equal volume cells contain different masses, so their mass per unit volume differs.

blocks.heading: Volume conversions are cubed
content: A length conversion acts once, but a volume conversion acts in three dimensions. Since 1 cm = 10^-2 m, one cubic centimetre is (10^-2 m)^3 = 10^-6 m^3. Therefore 1 m^3 = 10^6 cm^3.
This gives a useful density conversion. A density of 1 g cm^-3 means 10^-3 kg in 10^-6 m^3, which is 10^3 kg m^-3. So multiply a value in g cm^-3 by 1000 to express it in kg m^-3.
A reliable method is to convert mass and volume separately into one consistent system before substituting. This is safer than trying to repair a mixed-unit answer afterward.

figure.purpose: Make the cubed length conversion and density conversion visually explicit.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper conversion ladder. First show 1 cm equals 10^-2 m, then three dimension arrows leading to 1 cm cubed equals 10^-6 m cubed. Below, show 1 g cm^-3 equals 1000 kg m^-3 by converting numerator and denominator separately. Use distinct colours for mass and volume factors.
figure.alt_text: A conversion ladder cubes the centimetre-to-metre factor for volume and derives the density conversion.

blocks.heading: From dimensions to density
content: A solid cylindrical sample has diameter 1.20 cm, length 8.00 cm and mass 25.0 g. First convert to SI units: radius r = 0.00600 m, length L = 0.0800 m and mass m = 0.0250 kg.
The geometric volume is V = pi r^2 L = pi(0.00600 m)^2(0.0800 m) = 9.05 x 10^-6 m^3. Now use rho = m/V = 0.0250 kg divided by 9.05 x 10^-6 m^3 = 2.76 x 10^3 kg m^-3.

Check independently in centimetre units. The volume is pi(0.600 cm)^2(8.00 cm) = 9.05 cm^3, so the density is 25.0 g divided by 9.05 cm^3 = 2.76 g cm^-3. Multiplying by 1000 gives the same 2.76 x 10^3 kg m^-3.

figure.purpose: Model a complete dimensions-to-volume-to-density calculation with an independent unit-system check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout. Left: an annotated cylinder with diameter 1.20 cm, length 8.00 cm and mass tag 25.0 g. Centre: SI conversion and volume steps. Right: density result and a separate centimetre-and-gram check arriving at the matching converted result. Keep every unit visible.
figure.alt_text: A cylinder's dimensions give its volume, which combines with mass to calculate density in two consistent unit systems.

blocks.heading: Material volume is not always outer volume
content: It is tempting to multiply the largest length, width and height of every object and call that its material volume. That works for a complete cuboid, so the shortcut feels reasonable.

It fails for a bracket with a cut-out, a hollow tube or any object with empty space inside its outer boundary. Density relates mass to the volume of material actually present, not automatically to the whole bounding box.

For a 0.540 kg aluminium bracket with density 2700 kg m^-3, the material volume is V = m/rho = 2.00 x 10^-4 m^3. If its outer box occupies 3.00 x 10^-4 m^3, the difference is empty space or removed material, not a change in the aluminium's density.

figure.purpose: Correct confusion between an object's bounding volume and the volume of material present.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison panel. Draw one complete cuboid and one L-shaped bracket inside dashed bounding boxes of the same outer dimensions. Shade only the material. Label bounding volume and material volume without adding pressure, buoyancy or molecular language.
figure.alt_text: A complete cuboid fills its bounding box, while a bracket contains less material than its outer box suggests.

blocks.heading: The density route
content: Start by deciding which quantity is unknown: density, mass or material volume. Choose rho = m/V, m = rho V or V = m/rho without changing the physical meaning.

Next identify the volume of material. Use supplied geometry when the object is solid and regular, or rearrange the density formula when mass and material density are known. Convert all quantities to consistent units before substitution.

Finish with two checks. Confirm that the unit matches the unknown, then ask whether the direction of the comparison makes sense: more mass in the same volume means greater density, while the same mass in less volume also means greater density. Stop here before pressure, hydrostatic effects or upthrust.

figure.purpose: Compress density calculations and checks into a reusable decision route.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper flow strip: choose unknown, identify material volume, choose rearrangement, convert units, substitute, check unit and comparison. Include small icons for a solid cylinder, a cut-out bracket and a balance. Keep pressure and fluid imagery absent.
figure.alt_text: A six-step route selects the unknown, finds material volume, converts units and checks a density calculation.

concepts_taught: Density as mass per unit volume
Difference between material volume and bounding volume
misconceptions_addressed: A length conversion factor can be used unchanged for volume.
The outer bounding volume of every object equals its material volume.
A larger mass always means a greater density without considering volume.
